4.6. “Thus, Ānanda, it was said: ‘One who possesses three qualities is deposited in heaven as if brought there. What are the three? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the first quality that one must possess so that, being endowed with it, one is deposited in heaven as if brought there. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu has learned much, remembers what he has heard, and accumulates what he has heard—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legends, birth stories, marvelous accounts, and classifications—that is, the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and which reveals the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life. This is the second quality that one must possess so that, being endowed with it, one is deposited in heaven as if brought there. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu has attained the four jhānas—states of sublime happiness in the present life—which belong to the higher mind and are to be realized by one’s own direct knowledge. This is the third quality that one must possess so that, being endowed with it, one is deposited in heaven as if brought there.

Thus, Ānanda, it was said: ‘One who possesses three qualities is deposited in heaven as if brought there. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “One who is virtuous, learned, and a master of the jhānas, Is deposited in heaven, like one carried there. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “It would be good, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, if you were to practice for the sake of the destruction of craving, abandoning delight and lust, then, by the destruction of craving, you would be freed from suffering. This is the summary of the Dhamma taught in brief by the Tathāgata. “But, Bhante, how does one know, how does one see, so that, by the destruction of craving, one is freed from suffering? “Ānanda, whatever is felt here, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, that is conditioned by contact. By knowing and seeing this thus, Ānanda, by the destruction of craving, one is freed from suffering. “But, Bhante, how does one know, how does one see, so that one knows and sees: ‘This is conditioned by contact’? “Ānanda, whatever is felt here, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, that is conditioned by name-and-form. By knowing and seeing this thus, Ānanda, by the destruction of craving, one is freed from suffering. “But, Bhante, how does one know, how does one see, so that one knows and sees: ‘This is conditioned by name-and-form’? “Ānanda, whatever is felt here, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, that is conditioned by consciousness. By knowing and seeing this thus, Ānanda, by the destruction of craving, one is freed from suffering. “But, Bhante, how does one know, how does one see, so that one knows and sees: ‘This is conditioned by consciousness’? “Ānanda, whatever is felt here, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, that is conditioned by formations. By knowing and seeing this thus, Ānanda, by the destruction of craving, one is freed from suffering. “But, Bhante, how does one know, how does one see, so that one knows and sees: ‘This is conditioned by ignorance’? “Ānanda, when one knows and sees thus, one knows and sees: ‘This is conditioned by ignorance. The Section on Legal Procedure (Vyavahārakāṇḍa)
Invocation: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva."

Having heard those various eloquent words of his— words made clear by the path of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) such as logic (*nyāya*), and established by the power of wisdom skilled in investigating the doctrines of diverse scriptures—
the learned scholars experience horripilation at every step.
In this twelfth chapter, Lakṣmīdhara extends his legal discourse.
In that regard, the king's first duty is the inspection of legal proceedings;
immediately after that follows the instruction of the presiding judge, the court officials, and the members of the assembly.

Now follows the determination of legal proceedings: Desiring to examine legal cases, the king, humble and accompanied by Brahmins as well as ministers skilled in counsel, shall enter the court.
Seated there, or even standing, with his right hand raised and wearing modest dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal cases of the litigants.
Day by day, through reasons observed in the world and those found in the scriptures,
[these matters] were recorded separately within the eighteen branches of learning.
Having taken his seat upon the Dharma-seat, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed,
he should bow to the world-protectors and begin the examination of the case.

"Desirous of seeing the legal proceedings"— that is, desirous of determining the subjects of dispute between the plaintiff and the defendant—

18. The meaning is that the king should examine legal cases strictly in accordance with the *dharmaśāstra*. Furthermore, he should do so together with learned *brāhmaṇas*.

Even though the *brāhmaṇas* are the speakers, their utility lies solely in being assistants to the king; for it is the king alone who possesses the power to inflict punishment or grant favor. For this very reason, it is said that he must be "free from anger and greed. Even if he is capable, he must act in accordance with the *dharmaśāstra*, and not otherwise under the influence of anger and the like.

The meaning is that it must be treated [as such]. Even though the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is singular, the plural number is used in reference to the specific distinctions within its own body—as in the term *viśvarūpa*.

The one who takes the wife shall pay the debt. Then, in the absence of both the taker of the wife and the taker of the wealth, the son alone [discharges] the debt incurred by the father, due to the connection arising from the seed.

"He shall pay" means: when there is no one to take the wealth, no son exists, and the wife alone—deprived of both wealth and sons—has entered another's house; then, in the absence of both the wealth-taker and the son, the woman-taker shall pay the debt. For in the Soma sacrifices, there are sixteen priests; among them, four are "principal"—the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, [the Brahman, and the Udgātṛ].

"Brahmā and Udgātṛ"—this constitutes half of them. Since their sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is one hundred and twelve, half of that is fifty-six. By half of that again—namely, twenty-eight—they are the "half-sharers" (*ardhinaḥ*). "The others" refers to those whose appointment is prescribed immediately after that: the Maitrāvaruṇa, Pratiprasthātṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Prastotṛ. "Third-sharers" (*tṛtīyinaḥ*) means they receive a third part. The word *aṃśa* has the same meaning as the word *ardha*; the term *ardha* itself [is used here].

It is not necessarily an equal division; it also applies by way of proximity even when there is a slight deficiency or excess. Therefore, sixteen are taken from fifty-six as the third part. Thus, there are four for each. They grant the entire third part of the *tīrtha* and also the third part of fifty-six. The *acchāvāka* belongs to the *hotṛ*, the *neṣṭṛ* to the *adhvaryu*, the *abhiṣṭhātṛ* to the *brahman*, and the *pratihartṛ* to the *udgātṛ*. And those who receive a quarter-share (*pādinaḥ*) receive a fourth part.

They perform the ritual action, thus they are called "pādinas" (those who take a quarter). And in the fourth position, at the end of the station of the Maitrāvaruṇa, there is a "fourth part" within the group of twelve, as before. A man who, having been summoned by the king’s officers, does not go to give evidence when he is present, shall be declared a liar and shall incur the sin of perjury. 419. He who, being capable of giving evidence, remains silent, or he who, having given false testimony, subsequently admits its truth, both shall be punished as liars. 420. False testimony given through lust, anger, fear, friendship, greed, ignorance, or childishness must be corrected by the king with various punishments. 421. When a witness gives testimony contrary to what he saw or heard, whether out of his own accord or at the instigation of another, he falls from heaven after death and incurs hell. 422. False testimony destroys the offspring, cattle, heaven, and fame; therefore, one should never give false testimony in any matter whatsoever. 423. False testimony concerning small cattle destroys the offspring; that concerning large cattle destroys one's cattle; that concerning land destroys one's heaven; that concerning gold destroys one's fame. 424. False testimony concerning human beings destroys all; therefore, one should never give false testimony regarding any matter whatsoever. 425. By false testimony concerning water, one is born a fish; by false testimony concerning land, a frog; by false testimony concerning fire, a vulture; by false testimony concerning gold, a crow. 426. By false testimony concerning honey or clarified butter, one becomes a wasp; by false testimony concerning clothes, a crane; by false testimony concerning elephants, horses, or carriages, a camel. 427. By false testimony concerning cows, one becomes a donkey; by false testimony concerning sesame seeds, a rat; by false testimony concerning grain, a partridge; by false testimony concerning silver, a blue jay. 428. By false testimony concerning a garment, one becomes a peacock; by false testimony concerning a woman, a lizard; by false testimony concerning a man, a village pig; by false testimony concerning clarified butter, a cormorant. 429. By false testimony concerning honey, one becomes a bee; by false testimony concerning lead or tin, a woodpecker; by false testimony concerning cotton, a crane; by false testimony concerning silk or wool, a fly. 430. By false testimony concerning other minor matters, one becomes a cricket; thus have I declared the various births resulting from false testimony in this world. 431. One should speak the truth when asked in court, exactly as it was seen or heard; by speaking the truth, one attains both worlds; there is no higher duty than the truth. 432. Truth is the very foundation of the Vedas, of the sacrificial offerings, and of the oblations; truth is said to be the highest duty; therefore, one should always speak the truth. 433. "After death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist. Gautama said: "Vāseṭṭha, these questions have not been declared by me as undeclared. Vāseṭṭha asked: "But why, Gautama, have these been left undeclared? Gautama replied: "Because they do not conduce to the goal, because they do not lead to detachment, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nirvāṇa; therefore, I have left them undeclared. Vāseṭṭha asked: "But what, Gautama, has been declared by you as declared? Gautama replied: "This is suffering—this has been declared by me as declared. This is the origin of suffering—this has been declared by me as declared. This is the cessation of suffering—this has been declared by me as declared. This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering—this has been declared by me as declared. Vāseṭṭha asked: "Why, Gautama, has this been declared by you as declared? Gautama replied: "Because it conduces to the goal, because it leads to detachment, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nirvāṇa; therefore, I have declared it. Vāseṭṭha said: "Excellent, Gautama! Excellent, Gautama! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by Gautama in many ways. Now, Vāseṭṭha, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Well-Gone One, a Knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a Teacher of gods and humans, an Awakened One, a Blessed One—he, having realized it through his own super-knowledge, proclaims this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, its generation with its recluses and brahmins, its gods and humans. One should take vessels containing grain for his instruction. When the milk has been boiled, having washed, smeared, and polished the metallic vessels, and having performed the sweeping and plastering of the house, the prompt for the Vaiśvadeva rite is given as the occasion for bathing.
Having bathed, put on two white garments, washed his hands and feet, stepped out, and sipped water, he enters the temple of the gods.

Having entered and paid homage, having kindled the fire in the sanctuary, and having brought together fuel-sticks, *darbha* grass, flowers, the sacrificial offering (*bali*), and the vessel for the propitiatory rite (*śāntipātra*), he should sprinkle the food with clarified butter, as well as whatever else is required for the daily rites. He should offer oblations to the gods in the marriage fire and present the *bali* to the wives of the gods at the husband's direction. Once the offerings to the gods and guests have been performed, he should satisfy his householders and disciples according to their respective roles.
